speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just a few comments to make on the estimates now before us, the estimates of the Department of National Revenue.
I fully agree with the statements of the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) on charitable donations. For four years now we have been insisting every time these
DEBATES	4825
Supply-National Revenue estimates were before us, on overall legislation to cover charitable donations in a uniform manner all across Canada.
The law now provides that a taxpayer is entitled to donate up to 10 per cent of his net income and claim a deduction for that same amount. Now, in every case submitted to us in the past few years, most taxpayers who have complained to me claimed exemptions around 6 or 7 per cent of their income.
In nearly 90 per cent of these cases, the officials of the Department of National Revenue did not allow these claims, did not accept the exemptions claimed, or they granted the taxayers an exemption from $100 to $150, to which any taxpayer is entitled.
Now, if usages and customs of the officials of the Revenue Department are not to accept these receipts or these claims for charitable donations, it should be so stated in the house and not proceeded with secretly, in an underhanded way, as hypocrites, to make people believe that the Income Tax Act, as far as charitable donations are concerned, is generous to the Canadians who are making these donations to charitable institutions.
Mr. Chairman, the minister is well aware of the situation. I would suggest that the act be made uniform. Instead of saying that a taxpayer is entitled to give up to 10 per cent of his income for charitable donations, if it is felt that 10 per cent is too high, this should be reduced to 5 or 6 per cent, but it should be the same for all, for the whole population, so that everyone would be entitled to it. At present, everyone is not entitled to it. First, I note that the exemptions of $200 to $250 are not allowed this year.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Furthermore, I am told that from now on those charitable organizations must be recognized by the federal government.
But the legislation is not clear on that point. Will parish priests have to apply for a licence? Will they be given a collar to wear around their neck when they are issued a licence authorizing them to receive charitable donations? How does the government intend to apply that legislation? What does he mean by organizations recognized by the federal government? What will have to be done to be recognized? That is with regard to donations to charitable organizations.
Mr. Chairman, charitable donations are not made only in rectories. They are made outside also, for instance, to the Red Cross, any welfare association in a parish, the Boy Scouts or any tag day or apple sale. I think that people who give $1, $2 or $5 on such
4826	COMMONS
Supply-National Revenue occasions are making charitable donations. Social clubs, such as the Richelieu, Rotary and Kiwanis clubs who work tor underprivileged children, the poor, are charitable organizations-I am sure of that-but such receipts are not accepted. The money given to those people is not allowed. I think that the Income Tax Act is impossible to understand and can be taken to mean this or that, so that everyone is at sea. Even the minister does not understand the situation and we tolerate such administration.
With regard to another matter, I must say that for four years I have been asking the Minister of National Revenue to allow workers to deduct from their income the money spent to buy the tools they need for their work in any industry whatsoever. For instance, a mechanic should be allowed to deduct from his total income the cost of the tools he needs to work at his trade, and the same privilege should be given to construction workers, carpenters, woodworkers. Nothing is being done. There is discrimination there.
A doctor who buys office equipment, instruments, lancets to operate, can deduct such expenditures from his income, because it is considered that he needs them to practise his profession. But workers, carpenters, woodworkers, mechanics also have the right to purchase tools to work at their trade.
Why is such discrimination practised against the workers, against those who earn their living as honestly as any doctor or lawyer? And yet the doctor or the lawyer has the right to deduct from his income expenditures made to purchase office equipment or instruments.
Another thing. A doctor who must make visits, has an office 50 miles away and must travel by car, has the right to deduct his travelling expenses to practise his profession outside his house.
Strangely enough, a workman using his car in his work, in any industry, is not allowed to deduct travelling expenses from his revenue. He is told it is a normal means of transport. Is it not the same for a lawyer or a doctor? Why is this not considered by the Minister of National Revenue? These are facts and, in many cases, the income tax department makes arbitrary decisions concerning citizens as responsible as those allowed an income tax exemption or deduction.
Mr. Chairman, we have also called the minister's attention to the basic exemptions, from the income tax point of view. At the
[Mr. Caouette.l
DEBATES	May 6, 1966
moment, the government allows an exemption of $1,000 for single people and $2,000 for married people. We have been suggesting for a long time that this be increased to $2,500 and $5,000 respectively. Since taxes are necessary, let us tax those who have the means to pay and not those who do not.
There are, in Canada, United States industries and Americans who make money out of our natural resources and pay nothing or next to nothing to the Canadian government for their operations. These are the people who should fill the pockets of the Minister of National Revenue instead of the workers, the miners, the small settlers, the farmers, ordinary people who work developing our resources for the benefit of foreigners. Why not tax those who have the means, those who benefit most from the development of our natural resources, instead of taxing those who work like mercenaries for foreigners in Canada.
I understand the Minister of National Revenue has a huge income in comparison to his expenditures which are not too high. We are asked to give him a further $94,565,800, increasing his revenue to something like $9 billion. The administrative expenses of this department are not excessive.
Before resuming my seat, however, I should like to draw the attention of the minister to another point. Last March 23, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather) asked the government what its revenue was from the sale of liquor, lager, ale, spirits and wine. According to the minister's answer, in 1965 lager brought in $106,394,832 in excise duties, spirits $145,268,424, and wine $4,204,677, for a grand total of $225,867,933. Furthermore, from January to October 1965 only, liquor imports brought in $27,668,505 in customs duties. Thus excise and customs duties together brought in a total of 252 million. A note at the bottom of the answer on page 3047 of Hansard for March 23, 1966 says:
Above revenue figures do not include the 11 per cent federal sales tax which also applies but is not identifiable with specific commodities.
Mr. Chairman, imagine an 11 per cent tax on the sales total. What a fantastic sum this tax must bring the Department of National Revenue.
In answer to the question of the hon. member for New Westminster who wanted to know whether the government was spending money to encourage public temperance and
May 6, 1966

support programs fighting against alcoholism, the government said:
Insofar as the Department of National Health and Welfare is concerned, expenditure on promotion of temperance and supporting anti-alcoholic programs was nil.
We make tremendous expenditures to enlarge hospitals and to cure sick people, tor instance, and this is in order. But nothing to educate the people. This is what I want to emphasize. I realize that it is perhaps not for the Department of National Revenue to decide on broadcasts over the C.B.C., but I would ask the minister, who perhaps gets $500 or $600 million a year from alcoholic beverage consumption alone, to impress on his colleagues that they should urge the government to have the C.B.C. provide free time so as to educate our younger people, and adults too, on the importance of temperance in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I know that it is not the Department of National Revenue which will decide on such programs, but I wanted to point out to the house on how profitable the consumption or sale of alcoholic beverages in Canada is for the Department of National Revenue.
As far as the expenditures of this department are concerned, as I said, they are not excessive, as compared to the income which pours into the coffers of the said department.
In conclusion, I should like to repeat that, for instance, the section of the act governing charitable donations should be applied uniformly so that all Canadians without exception might be treated the same without any discrimination. This is the first point.
Second point: Our workers should be entitled to deduct from their income the cost of the equipment used in their profession.
Third point: Travelling expenses of workers being transferred, whether they use their own car or public transportation facilities, as in the case of doctors, lawyers, engineers or any other social class should be deductible.
Finally, we ask that basic exemptions be increased from $1,000 to $2,000 for unmarried persons and from $2,500 to $5,000 for married people and heads of families.
If such significant basic exemptions are granted to our workers, then the government will be able to claim that it has rendered a service, not only to one class of society, but to the whole country, because, in the final analysis, if workers have more money to spend, it is obvious that a large part of this money will return to the national treasury, since taxes
Supply-National Revenue are collected at every level of the Canadian economy.
The minister should consider this. Every year, he promises to do so, but once the year is over, he fails to keep his promises and to look effectively into the problem so as to achieve results.
Mr. Chairman, I sincerely believe that the Income Tax Act can be adjusted and adapted to the needs of the Canadian people, instead of taking advantage of them as at present.
Let this act be amended so as to deal fairly with the little people as well as the rich and vice versa, but let everyone be treated fairly.

Mr. Chairman,
32 years ago next month I started my first job, that of assistant private secretary to the then minister of national revenue. Since that time I have had what might be described as a filial feeling for the department and a most sympathetic understanding of the dedicated public servants who make up its staff. Consequently, to participate briefly in discussion of these estimates brings some nostalgic memories.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has mentioned that this is the first time the estimates of the department have been presented to the committee since the retirement of David Sim, the former deputy minister for customs and excise. To members of this house of all parties, Dave Sim, for many years the dean of deputies, was a model and an example to all public servants. I say to you, sir, that Canada has never had a more devoted, knowledgeable, impartial and intelligent deputy minister, and certainly not one so understanding and responsive to the role of parliament and of members of parliament. The process of handing down farms from generation to generation is jeopardized by this tax. The desire of agricultural departments to propagate paying and functioning farm units is also jeopardized. May 6, 1966

Mr. Chairman, I will not take too much time. I simply want to share my impressions on the income tax form.
I believe this form should be redesigned, because as it now stands, it entails certain inequities.
First, there are two forms: one for individuals and one for institutions and corporations. Why two forms? Why not make them more simple and combine them into one? Only one form, so that everyone would be on the same footing. If there are now different classes in society who enjoy some protection from the Department of National Revenue, that is not equitable. It is not fair. If some citizens are paying too much tax while others are not paying enough, let us have an adequate form and let it be used by everyone and let everyone be treated on the same footing.
It is not because I am in favor of taxes. On the contrary, deep in my mind I think taxes are robbery, and the way in which they are collected from the individuals is depriving them of the purchasing power they need for their livelihood. Some people who pay their taxes are unable to pay their debts. And it is considered normal to make them pay their taxes and to leave their debts outstanding.
Supply-National Revenue
There are small companies and small industries that have paid a lot of taxes and that are unable to meet their debts, while some large companies have a certain separate tax and pay less, and they are entitled to build up reserves, declared and undeclared reserves. They are not overly bothered, those reserves are not declared. In addition, there are four or five kinds of reserves, allowing these institutions to invest money in other places, on the stock market for instance, or in other bodies which do not pay any taxes and which are passed off as capital surplus which is not taxable. That is where the tax form should be redesigned in order to put everyone on the same footing. There should be some degree of justice in the tax form so that everybody would be equal and on the same footing.
In the province of Quebec, for instance, as concerns the sales tax, those who collect that tax for the province of Quebec are receiving 2 per cent.
Well, the federal government has the taxes collected by industrialists, businessmen, employers and those employers are required-the tax forms are so complicated and the situation is so involved-to pay accountants, qualified men to collect the tax and prepare tax returns.
In the case of the general tax collection, the income tax or the 11 per cent tax and others which the federal government levies, nothing is given to those people who are collecting for the federal government.
If the province of Quebec has seen fit to give 2 per cent, why should the federal government not give something to the industrialists or the individuals for collecting? This would prevent an increase in the cost of goods. All those operations are included in the cost of goods. It is always the little people who stand the racket and pay taxes.
When one considers the taxes paid by corporations and individuals, one finds that individuals and workers pay much more than corporations. There are approximately 80,000 corporations in Canada. There are large corporations with a big turn-over which invest billions and hundreds of millions of dollars, and yet pay much fewer taxes than the Canadian workers. This is unfair, and that is why I say there should be only one income tax return form, a simple one, simplified in all respects. Let us simplify it as much as possible and we shall give satisfaction.
With regard to the 11 per cent tax and other taxes collected, I should like to point
4836	COMMONS
Supply-National Revenue out to the minister or his representative that industrialists or businessmen who sustain losses have to pay the 11 per cent tax just the same. If people go bankrupt, if the situation is confused, it is because the system is defective. It forces people to go bankrupt and compels them to pay the 11 per cent tax just the same.
I would ask the minister to consider the matter of bankruptcies, because small businessmen or dealers who suffer such losses also have to pay the tax. This is further injustice. This tax should be deducted from the loss. The state must be able to take its share of bankruptcies just like individuals, small companies or small industrialists.
I would have many things to say on tax collection in Canada. There are so many kinds of taxes, direct and indirect, that we do not know which way to turn. The taxpayer pays more taxes than what it costs him for his living. It costs him less to live than the taxes he pays. The citizens are so taxed now that taxes will have to be reduced, because they are much too high. Instead of being reduced, they are increased, and at the same time, the cost of living is rising. The government creates inflation because of the taxes it levies. In the case of those who charge excessive rates of interest, nobody protests against that, against these companies; there is something wrong in our economic situation. The governments are now endorsing and protecting high finance. And the people are fleeced. The people are on the verge of bankruptcy. The people are so heavily taxed and indebted that they do not see the day when they will be able to get out of it.
For some years we have been saying that there is prosperity in Canada. It is because the government and the citizens have been allowed to run into debt that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has to impose restrictions on credit and investments; citizens are too heavily indebted.

The Minister of National Revenue should open his eyes. This concludes my remarks.

He said: In 1943, Mr. Speaker, the parliament of Canada passed the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act, which I now seek to repeal. The reasons for the initial passage of the bill were outlined by Hon. Mr. Crerar, who was then minister of mines and resources in the Liberal
[The Chairman.]
government of that day, as found on page 4921 of Hansard for July 16, 1943
To go back a little, a question arose as to the ownership of the minerals which might he found on lands transferred to the dominion in British Columbia and a test case was taken to the Privy Council to decide the ownership of the precious metals. The Privy Council gave judgment that the precious metals belonged to the crown in the right of the province.
Then, Mr. Hanson, the then hon. member for York-Sunbury, asked the minister for the citation, and Hon. Mr. Crerar went on to say:
The case was decided in 1889. An extract from the judgment of the Privy Council reads:
"The precious metals in, upon and under crown lands, are not incidents of the land but belong to the crown, and under section 109 of the British North America Act, 1867, beneficially to the province".
That judgment, of course, established that if precious metals were found on such lands, the dominion had no claim to any benefits arising from the exploitation of these precious metals.
Having read these words of Mr. Crerar, I want to go on to indicate that, in my view, Mr. Crerar misrepresented the judgment of the Privy Council. Parliament was led to believe that certain things existed when, in fact, they did not. In the first place, the Privy Council decision of 1889, to which reference was made, had nothing whatever to do with Indian reserve lands as such. This decision was related to the land grants or the 40-mile swath of land which was given to the Canadian Pacific in consideration for building the railroad and carrying out one of the terms of union between British Columia and Canada.
The matter came to a head when gold was discovered in 1884 in an area within this 40 mile land grant. A dispute arose as to the proprietory ownership of gold. This was the case that went to the Privy Council. Under section 92 of the British North America Act, which gives jurisdiction to the provinces, certain things are exempted from provincial jurisdiction, such as railways which are interprovincial. Section 91 of the B.N.A. Act, part 24, specifically gives exclusive jurisdiction to the parliament of Canada in the matter of Indians and lands reserved for Indians.
If I recall the quotation from Mr. Crerar, in 1943 the government of that day took the 1889 decision of the Privy Council related to lands conveyed by the dominion and applied it to Indian reserves. They distorted the position of the Privy Council, either deliberately or otherwise. The matter which was
May 6, 1966

before the Privy Council related to the railway and the terms of union between the province of British Columbia and Canada, and the issue with which the Privy Council concerned itself was the words "public lands". In giving this citation I submit that Hon. Mr. Crerar misrepresented what the Privy Council did. I should like to read a portion of the Privy Council judgment as found on page 306 of The Law Reports, Appeal Cases, 1889:
Their Lordships are for these reasons of the opinion that the judgment appealed from must be reversed, and that it ought to be declared that the precious metals within the railway belt are vested in the crown, subject to the control and disposal of the government of British Columbia, and they will humbly advise Her Majesty to that effect.
The decision of the Privy Council specifically spelled out in this way was concerned with precious metals within the railway belt. This decision of the Privy Council reversed previous decisions by the Exchequer Court of Canada and the Supreme Court of Canada, which held that these precious metals were within the domain of the dominion government. There was in 1943 a deliberate conspiracy of arrogation on the part of the federal government and on the part of the provincial government as well. We must remember that the federal government was the Liberal party in office. In British Columbia in those days we had a coalition government, which was a marriage of convenience between the Liberals and the Conservatives. In that coalition government the Liberals were in majority. The individual who was the then minister of mines in British Columbia was the late Hon. Ernest Carson, who was a Conservative in that coalition.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The people in that government, on the basis of having misrepresented the decision of the Privy Council in London, undertook to deal arrogantly with the rights of our native Indian people in British Columbia, in so far as mineral resources are concerned.
At no time could I find any reference in the speeches in Hansard, either of the House of Commons or of the Senate, when this matter was being considered, or indeed in any other documents or records, to any consultation or discussion with the native Indian peoples themselves. It was just a matter of the usual practice of governments running
Indian Affairs
rampant over the rights of a group of people who were in this country long before anybody else and who have, and I submit still have in British Columbia, the original rights to the land and to the resources.
I think that the schedule to the bill passed in 1943 misled parliament in at least three respects. In the preliminary part of it there are four whereases, the first of which was misleading, and I want to show to what extent. I shall read it:
Whereas from time to time treaties have been made with the Indians for the surrender for various considerations of their personal and usufruc-tury rights to territories now included in the province of British Columbia, such considerations including the setting apart for the exclusive use of the Indians of certain definite areas of land known as Indian reserves:
That statement and that whereas is grossly misleading, because we know that the number of treaties in effect in British Columbia is relatively few and affects only a very small portion of the landed area, and of the people themselves. By and large the native Indian people in British Columbia have never entered into any treaty with any government over their land. It was simply a matter of encroachment by European settlers and by the government of those days on to the land held by the native Indian people from time immemorial.
Sir, the first whereas is false and misleading because it leaves the impression that treaties have been made to set aside certain landed areas as reserves, and such was not the case.
The second whereas says:
And whereas the said Indian reserves were conveyed to the dominion government as trustee for the Indians under the terms and conditions set forth in an agreement dated the 24th day of September, 1912, between the dominion government and the province of British Columbia;
That is misleading because it follows the first whereas, and the implication is that this was done with the consent of and by the agreement of the Indian native peoples in British Columbia. The facts of the matter are that it was not.
Never at any time have the native peoples in British Columbia agreed to accept the so-called agreement of 1912, the findings of the McKenna-McBride Royal Commission, the provisions of the Indian Land Settlement Act, or any of the unilateral means used by government for its purposes. There has not been one iota of agreement by the Indian

May 6, 1966
Indian Affairs
peoples to the one-sided approabh that dealt with their original hereditary land claims.
The third whereas is misleading also, because it says as follows:
And whereas the precious metals in, upon, or under the lands comprising such reserves are not incidents of such lands but belong beneficially to the crown in the right of the province of British Columbia with the result that the development of all the minerals in, upon or under such lands is at present impractical since the precious and base metals are closely associated and cannot be mined separately;
That is misleading because it takes the 1889 decision of the Privy Council that related to the C.P.R. land grants and says that, in effect, that decision applied to Indian reserves. Such was not the case.
Based upon that an agreement was signed to deal arbitrarily with the rights of the native Indian people with respect to their mineral resources. The effect of that was shown in a document recently circulated by the Indian affairs branch under date January 18, 1965, dealing with this matter. It points out that before the mineral resources of any reserves can be developed they must-and there is no question about this; the document asserts the term-they must be surrendered. In other words, in order for mineral resources on any Indian reserve to be developed today, under the terms of the agreement which was ratified in 1943 by the law which I now seek to repeal, it was made a mandatory provision that the Indian peoples must give up their rights to these resources, must toss them to one side, must surrender them and no longer have any rights in them.
This surrender is then followed by the administration of the resource itself being given to the government of the Province of British Columbia, and the relevant law of that province being made applicable. The income from any of the operations of mining or leasing, or from prospectors' licenses or the like, in fact the income from any such activity is, under the agreement, divided 50-50 between the province of British Columbia and the government of Canada.
It is interesting to note that the government of Canada persistently has claimed that it exercises that income and administers it in trust for the Indian Band concerned. It is interesting to note, too, that in the whole period of time since 1943, since this agreement has been in effect, the total amount of money that has accrued from the exploration or exploitation of mineral resources on Indian 
reserves in British Columbia has come to the grand total of $10 exactly. There is $6.25 from one reserve, and $3.25 from another.
However, as the memorandum of the Indian affairs branch dated January 18, 1965, points out, a tremendous amount of interest has developed in the last year to two in mineral resources and mineral exploration in British Columbia. The Indian affairs branch points out that there has been an increasing interest in the mineral resource potential on Indian reserves in British Columbia, and that this interest may serve to accelerate in developing these resources.
This parliament should want to repeal the act, for the reason that it was initially an imposition upon a group of people by unilateral action on the part of the government of Canada and the government of the province of British Columbia. The act was passed without consultation.
We are in an era now when there is an undivided opinion that the key to success for Indian peoples, and for their advancement, rests in their being able to control their own affairs. If we repeal this imposing legislation we shall return to the situation that existed prior to 1943 and we shall give to the Indian people the right to decide for themselves what they want to do with the mineral resources on their reserves. There was misinterpretation of a Privy Council decision. There was no consultation with the Indian people. In fact no advice was given to them about it. Parliament was misled, as I have indicated, and the question of land and mining resources has never been really settled.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The government has indicated on a number of occasions-although it has not done anything about it, yet-that it wishes to deal with this land question in a fair and just way. I submit that it is not possible to do so, and to meet the original and hereditary claims of the Indians of British Columbia, so long as this statute remains on the books. I sincerely hope that parliament will repeal this law at the earliest possible moment.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has spoken well on a public bill which is of considerable interest to Indians and reserve Indians in British Columbia. He has spoken with his usual feeling for the Indian people of the province, and with the capability he
May 6, 1966

always brings to a case in their interest when he speaks before this house.
I listened with a great deal of interest as he discoursed on this problem of mineral rights on Indian lands in British Columbia. The bill which he has brought before the house is a little bill which simply seeks the repeal of the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act. The hon. member for Skeena says in the explanatory note to his bill:
The agreement provides that the administration, control and disposal of all minerals and mineral claims, both precious and base, in, upon or under all Indian Reserves in British Columbia shall be subject to the laws of the province of British Columbia.
The agreement further provides that any revenues collected by the province of British Columbia in respect of any sale or other disposition of minerals and mineral claims shall be divided between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia on a 50/50 basis.
This is the purpose of the little bill, a measure which arises out of the historical background which has already been discussed by the hon. member for Skeena and which I intend to review to some extent, though possibly with the emphasis differently placed.
The province of British Columbia entered confederation in 1871. Clause 13 of the Articles of Union provided that the dominion would have charge of Indian affairs and that the province would from time to time convey to the dominion such lands as were required for reserves. The selection of lands for the Indians caused a great deal of trouble between the two governments and resulted in a number of commissions being set up either jointly or by each government separately. The matter was finally disposed of in 1938 by order in council 1036 of the Lieutenant Governor in Council of British Columbia, by which reserves were conveyed to the dominion.
From the very begining the dispute over surface rights involved mineral rights and the administration thereof, with both the dominion and province claiming jurisdiction. This dispute became even more complicated when in the precious metals case-Attorney General of B.C. v. Attorney General of Canada, 1889-the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council ruled that the precious metals, gold and silver, were vested in the crown in the right of the province.
The administration was then divided -precious metals to the province and
Indian Affairs
base metals to the dominion. The province later entered a claim for administration over the base metals as well. The bickering led to the passing in 1943 of the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act, by which administration of base mineral rights would pass to the province upon surrender by the Indians. This act settled no legal rights but was merely an attempt to place administration in one place since, with the previous divisions, no development could take place, as in British Columbia gold and silver are contained in almost all the ores of the remaining minerals.
Anyone who sets out to mine base metals in British Columbia finds he is involved not only in a base metal mine but in a gold mine and a silver mine. For this reason, dividing minerals into precious minerals and base minerals presented an impossible situation.
While the hon. member for Skeena was addressing the house and referring to the action of the federal government in respect of this matter of the British Columbia Indian Reserves Mineral Resources Act, I sent out for a copy of Hansard covering the debate from which he quoted, and I have before me the debates of the House of Commons for the session of 1943, volume 5. I wish to turn to the debate to which the hon. member referred. There was a good debate in the House of Commons that day. I see that the report begins on page 4920 and continues for several pages, to page 4927. A number of speakers took part, so it cannot be said that this little bill was cavalierly dealt with, or passed over very quickly by the parliament of that year. It received a good deal of consideration, and Hansard stands on record to that effect.
Hon. Mr. Crerar introduced the bill, and it is interesting to note that among those who entered the discussion was Mr. Coldwell the leader of the C.C.F. party in the house during that period. Another hon. member who played a considerable part and had a good deal to say about the bill-he finally called for it to be passed on division-was Mr. Neill, who was a long-time member for Co-mox-Alberni, whose able successor I see in his place in the house today. Mr. Neill was himself a member of the old C.C.F. party. Or was he an independent?-I stand to be corrected.

Mr. Neill was a well known member of the house. He was well known in B.C. and was quite a critic of the government of the day. He said, as recorded at page 4923 of Hansard for that year:
The general principle of this bill is undoubtedly good-*
He was raising some question in relation to the jurisdictional dispute going on, but he said:
The general principle of this bill is undoubtedly good because it does away with the objection that has been in existence for many years in British Columbia, that if the Indians-or anyone acting for them-discovered a valuable mine, it could never practically be worked because the other party, the provincial government or the dominion government, would step in and say, "You may take out your silver but you must not touch our lead, for instance."
This is the old problem of trying to work any claim, and the divided jurisdiction between base metals and precious metals, recognition that precious metals under Indian reserves belong to the crown in the right of British Columbia, and that development of all minerals, under the laws of Canada and British Columbia, independently, is impractical since precious and base metals cannot be mined separately.
The act also provided that as a matter of convenience, without affecting legal rights, the province of British Columbia should have charge of development of all minerals under the Indian reserves. It went on to provide that the administration and development of the minerals shall be subject to the laws of the province, following surrender pursuant to the Indian Act.
It went on to say that there should be no prospecting or right of entry to the Indian reserves until permission had been obtained from the Indian agent, and then it said that the agreement concerns only metallic minerals.

Since the effective date of the act, mineral surrenders to only six out of a total of 1,600 reserves in British Columbia have been approved by Indian bands, and none has been approved since 1950, which is a rather interesting note on the effectiveness of any program relating to the development of minerals under Indian lands in B.C.
Administrative responsibility for the use of the land resources is divided between the two governments, once a band has approved a mineral surrender. The mining or subsurface rights are administered by the B.C. government, whereas the rights to use land surface for mining purposes are administered by the federal government in consultation with the band council. There has been no development of mines on B.C. Indian lands, and exploratory work has been practically negligible.
The Indians' half share of revenues collected by the province would include only fees for recording claims and assessment work, etc., until such time as a mine had produced for three years, when it would become taxable under the British Columbia Mineral Taxation Act. There are no provisions for acreage rentals or cash bonuses on claims staked under B.C. legislation.
There have been discussions between the governments of B.C. and Canada in recent years, in fact within the last year or so, and progress is being made toward what is hoped to be a better situation for the Indians, and the administration of these lands for mining purposes.
In 1956 and 1957 discussions took place with the provincial deputy minister of mines in respect to interpretation of the act, and these led to some understandings which I will discuss. First, the revenue to be shared between the province and Canada, for band benefit, includes that collected under the Mining Income Tax Act by the province.
The band council could negotiate terms with an applicant for the use of surface for mining purposes, including payment to the band of acreage rental, cash bonus, amount per ton mined or a percentage of the value of mineral produced. On approval of terms, the band council could authorize the Indian agent to grant permission to the applicant to enter, prospect and stake claims on the reserve under the act and other provincial legislation.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
No serious exploration or development of mineral resources resulted from these understandings, so a formal approach was made to
Indian Affairs
the province of British Columbia for a revision of the agreement through an exchange of correspondence between ministers in 1961. My notes, in researching this, go on to say that the provincial ministers could not agree to transferring administration of minerals on Indian reserves to the federal government and, further, the province claimed ownership not only of precious metals, but also of base metals on some reserves. So the jurisdictional dispute continued. In particular was the fact that the province certainly did not want to see a situation in which two mining laws applied to the province, one which applied to commercial mining and one which now had sprung up under this act.
In subsequent discussions, Indian affairs officers produced evidence to invalidate the province's claim to base metals, and an appeal was made to leave questions of legal ownership unsettled in favour of reaching an agreement which would give the Indians in British Columbia similar benefits from minerals as was enjoyed in other provinces. At that time provincial officers found our general proposal unacceptable, but they offered no alternative proposal.
This is virtually where the negotiations stand today between the federal government and the province of British Columbia. I understand from the minister and from officers in the department that negotiations are going on steadily, that interviews have been held between officials of both governments and that to date no suitable solution has been found which would bring about a settlement of the question.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say I am as much in sympathy with the purposes of this bill as is my hon. friend. I am not certain that the simple repeal of the act, as he suggests, is the way to approach it. I think there will have to be further steps, and I believe these must be taken together. I think they have to be taken under the aegis of the government. There may be some question in respect of whether or not we are involving ourselves here in the handling of a money bill. I believe the government is aware that the problem exists. There is every evidence that it is being pursued by the dominion government and the provincial government, and that the government has at heart the interests of the Indian and native in working toward a solution of this problem.

Mr. Speaker, having seconded the bill introduced by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), I should like to say just a few words to indicate my support for it. I have been listening as closely as I could to the argument being advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman). In his analysis of the situation it would seem to me that he was in error in certain particulars at least, although I am glad to know he indicated his sympathy with the purposes of this bill. The hon. member had something to say about the matter of unification of mining laws in respect of mining operations in the province of British Columbia, regardless of the class of lands involved.
I should like to suggest to the hon. member, Mr. Speaker, that the act which the hon. member for Skeena is seeking to repeal really is not concerned with the question of a certain set of rules for the conduct of mining operations, but rather is concerned with a certain division of the revenue. It seems to me that this is the important principle involved in the proposal of the hon. member for Skeena-that is, that an error was committed by parliament in ratifying the agreement with the province of British Columbia and that grievous injury was done in fact by the province and its government of that day in seeking to impose this kind of jurisdiction on the Indian affairs branch on behalf of the Indian people of their full rights to the revenues from the properties.
This, to me, is the issue. Had there been some discussion with the Indian people in an effort to seek agreement that there be general application of the mining rules on their property similar to those which apply to mining operations in the province, then that might have been a proper field of negotiation for the province of British Columbia and perhaps the Indian affairs branch on behalf of the Indian people.
I submit there is a distinction there. I also would suggest that I might have a word to say here on the question that was raised by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). In doing so, may I say I certainly am, shall we say speaking on, layman's level to

the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. In this connection I should like to point out, with particular reference to the decision of the Privy Council on which apparently this original law was based, the distinction between lands in the railway belt and the Indian reserve lands which, to my layman's mind at least, appears to set out the very important distinction which has been established within the British North America Act itself.
In section 92 of the British North America Act, which has to do with the fields in which the legislatures of the provinces may exclusively make laws, we find in No. 10:
10. Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:
It mentions specifically railways and other works or other undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces. This, it seems to me, puts the situation in respect of any lands granted to a railway in a very different category from that in which the Indian reserve lands are placed by the British North America Act, because thereference to Indian reserve lands is set out very specifically in section 91, which deals with matters which lie exclusively within the jurisdiction of the federal authority. As has been mentioned in many discussions in relation to Indian problems in this house, it makes specific reference to Indians and lands reserved for the Indians.
In my understanding of the matter of land title, the basic rule is that unless there is a specific reservation in the title of the land for a specific purpose, such as the reservation of mineral rights, then the title to the land includes everything that is on it and under it. I am not going to go into the question of what may be above it. I think this is a pretty clear understanding. I know for example, in the title to my own property in Alberni, in respect of the E & N railway belt there is a specific reservation of mineral rights to the present owner, the C.P.R. It seems to my lay mind at least that this is the point the hon. member for Greenwood was raising in his question, and I felt that I should express it in lay language, with the hope that the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) would understand me and perhaps agree with me.

Mr. Speaker, my understanding is that under the terms of union with British Columbia and the original provinces which formed the Dominion of Canada, provision was made that the British North America Act of 1867 would apply. It is clearly stated in that act that Indian lands come under the jurisdiction of the federal government, as trustees for the Indian people.
My own view is that the province of British Columbia has always taken a very narrow and parsimonious approach to the rights of Indian peoples, and that the grounds on which it has chosen to involve itself in disputes as to Indian rights have created serious injustices to these native peoples. I think it is part of our responsibility in this house to make sure that this situation is reversed. If we intend to deal with the question referred to by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), the first thing we should do is repudiate these bad arrangements, which were agreed to probably with an incomplete understanding and appreciation for the rights of Indians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make one or two observations concerning the Eden valley Indians in southern Alberta. This land was purchased by the federal government in order to create a reserve. I am told that the mineral rights were reserved, which is distinctly different from what happened in respect of the mineral rights on other reservations, where they were retained in the name of the Indians in the form of a settlement made prior to 1905. I have in mind the situation regarding the Brocket, Gleichen and Sarcee reserves. I understand the Indians on these reserves possess the mineral rights.
It has always been my feeling that, since the federal government purchased those lands from private operators to create these Indian reserves, the Indians occupying these lands

should have the mineral rights. I rise at this time to speak on behalf of the Eden valley Indians and to place their difficulties, which have been brought to my attention on a number of occasions, before this house. I feel that these Indians should by all means have title to these mineral rights.
